title: Impact of Political Turnover on Public Spending

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Instrumental Variables (IV) regression using close-election Democratic wins as an instrument for Democratic control. This addresses the endogeneity problem where unobserved factors may simultaneously influence both Democratic control and public spending. The key assumptions are: (1) Relevance - close Democratic wins predict Democratic control, (2) Exclusion restriction - close wins only affect spending through their effect on Democratic control, and (3) Independence - close wins are as-good-as-random near the electoral threshold.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(AER)
library(stargazer)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s74_data.csv")

# Check data structure
head(data)
summary(data)

# First stage: Instrument relevance
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = data)
print("=== FIRST STAGE RESULTS ===")
print(summary(first_stage))
print(paste("F-statistic for instrument:", 
            summary(first_stage)$fstatistic[1]))

# Check instrument strength (F-stat > 10 rule of thumb)
f_stat <- summary(first_stage)$fstatistic[1]
print(paste("Instrument is", ifelse(f_stat > 10, "STRONG", "WEAK")))

# Second stage: IV regression
iv_model <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = data)
print("\n=== IV REGRESSION RESULTS ===")
print(summary(iv_model))

# Extract key coefficient
iv_coeff <- coef(iv_model)["x"]
iv_se <- summary(iv_model)$coefficients["x", "Std. Error"]
print(paste("\nMain Result: Democratic control increases log public spending by", 
            round(iv_coeff, 4)))
print(paste("Standard error:", round(iv_se, 4)))
print(paste("95% CI: [", round(iv_coeff - 1.96*iv_se, 4), ",", 
            round(iv_coeff + 1.96*iv_se, 4), "]"))

# Robustness checks
print("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECKS ===")

# 1. OLS comparison (biased but useful benchmark)
ols_model <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = data)
ols_coeff <- coef(ols_model)["x"]
print(paste("OLS coefficient:", round(ols_coeff, 4)))
print(paste("IV vs OLS difference:", round(iv_coeff - ols_coeff, 4)))

# 2. Reduced form (direct effect of instrument)
reduced_form <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = data)
rf_coeff <- coef(reduced_form)["z"]
print(paste("Reduced form coefficient:", round(rf_coeff, 4)))

# 3. Manual IV calculation (should match ivreg)
manual_iv <- rf_coeff / coef(first_stage)["z"]
print(paste("Manual IV coefficient:", round(manual_iv, 4)))

# 4. Test for weak instruments
print(paste("Cragg-Donald F-stat:", round(f_stat, 2)))

# 5. IV without controls (robustness)
iv_no_controls <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = data)
iv_coeff_no_controls <- coef(iv_no_controls)["x"]
print(paste("IV without controls:", round(iv_coeff_no_controls, 4)))

print("\n=== FINAL RESULT ===")
print(paste("CAUSAL EFFECT: Democratic control increases log public spending by", 
            round(iv_coeff, 4), "with SE =", round(iv_se, 4)))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a positive coefficient around 0.3-0.8, indicating that Democratic control increases public spending by approximately 30-80% (since y is in logs). This aligns with the conventional wisdom that Democratic governments tend to favor higher public spending on social programs, infrastructure, and public services compared to Republican governments. The IV estimate should be larger in magnitude than the OLS estimate if there's negative selection bias (i.e., Democrats tend to win in areas that would naturally have lower spending, creating downward bias in OLS).

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use close-election Democratic wins as an instrument for Democratic control.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests a negative causal impact of Democratic control on public spending.
